questions.q: What does "Think and Work Holistically" ask you to recognize?
options: That teams should always be reorganized into one combined department
That holistic thinking only applies to the service desk
That no service, practice, or team operates in isolation, and changes ripple outward across the system
That every decision requires sign-off from every department before proceeding
questions.explain: The lesson's example — a new incident-form field affecting reporting, knowledge articles, and automation — shows ripple effects that are easy to miss but not exotic.

questions.q: According to Keep It Simple and Practical, what should happen to a process step that doesn't add value?
options: It should be kept indefinitely because removing steps is always risky
It should be escalated to a steering committee for review every quarter
It should be duplicated across more teams to standardize it
It should be eliminated or simplified rather than defended because it already exists
questions.explain: ITIL 4 explicitly favors the minimum number of steps needed to accomplish an objective — complexity with no offsetting value is a pure cost.

questions.q: Why does Optimize and Automate insist that optimizing come before automating?
options: Because automating a broken process just makes it execute faster and fail more consistently
Because automation tools are always more expensive than manual labor
Because optimization makes automation technically impossible afterward
Because ITIL 4 prohibits automation of any manual process
questions.explain: The lesson's manual-approval-step example shows that automating a step kept alive only by a since-fixed tool limitation locks a flaw into permanence instead of removing it.

questions.q: What kind of work does this lesson say automation is genuinely valuable for?
options: Any process at all, regardless of volume or definition
Only processes that involve customer-facing communication
Work that has never been measured or reviewed
High-volume, repeatable, well-defined work that has already been assessed and streamlined
questions.explain: Examples given include routing routine service requests and auto-escalating overdue tickets — work suited to automation precisely because it's been optimized first.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the final three principles depend on the earlier four in the set of seven?
options: They don't depend on the earlier principles at all; each of the seven is fully independent
ITIL 4 requires principles to be applied in strict numerical order with no overlap

Holistic thinking needs the investigation from Start Where You Are, simplifying needs the visibility from Collaborate and Promote Visibility, and safe automation needs the feedback loops from Progress Iteratively With Feedback
The final three principles replace the need for the first four entirely
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties each of the final three back to a specific earlier principle, showing the seven are meant to be applied together, not picked one at a time.
